paragraphs.context: One snowy day in Connecticut, I wished I
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author traveled in her mind.
paragraphs.simple: On a snowy day in Connecticut, the author wanted to go to a sunny island. She was too busy for a holiday, so she traveled in her imagination. That is how she started this book about Hawaii.

background.note: A small state in the north-east of the USA, where the author lives. Winters there are cold and snowy.
A group of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Since 1959 it has been the 50th state of the USA.

paragraphs.context: In my research, I learned that the islands
paragraphs.simple: The islands began as volcanoes that rose from the sea. Over millions of years, birds and wind brought seeds. In the warm Pacific weather, plants, animals and insects grew well. The first people there were amazed.

background.note: The Pacific Ocean, the biggest ocean on earth, between Asia and America.

paragraphs.context: This is a big reason why I love
paragraphs.simple: The author loves her job because her imagination can take her anywhere, even to warm islands in winter. She hopes you will use your imagination to visit Hawaii too.

paragraphs.context: Aloha!
paragraphs.simple: "Aloha" is the Hawaiian word for hello, goodbye and love.

background.note: A Hawaiian word that means hello, goodbye and love. Say it ah-LOW-ha.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up town where Jack and Annie live. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the USA.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree
paragraphs.simple: The tree house can take Jack and Annie to the places in its books. While they are away, no time passes at home.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from King Arthur's Camelot. She travels through time and space and collects books.

background.note: King Arthur's castle and kingdom in old British stories.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie have many exciting adventures helping
paragraphs.mainIdea: They learn the art of magic.
paragraphs.simple: In books 25 to 28, Jack and Annie learn about magic.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie were sitting on their porch
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie were reading on their porch. Jack read about gorillas, and Annie read about Pilgrims.
paragraphs.tone: These are the places of their last two trips (books 26 and 27).

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” breathed Jack. He knew she was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie knows the tree house is back.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knew she meant the magic tree house. Annie always knew when it was back.

paragraphs.context: “We’re going to the woods!” he called through
paragraphs.simple: Jack called through the door that they had to check something in the woods.

paragraphs.context: He picked up his backpack. Then he and
paragraphs.simple: Jack took his backpack. They walked across the yard, then ran up their street into the woods.

paragraphs.context: In the last light of day, they hurried
paragraphs.simple: In the last daylight they hurried through the trees to the tallest oak. They stopped breathing for a moment as they looked up.

paragraphs.context: She started up the ladder. Jack followed. It
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house smells of summer.
paragraphs.simple: Annie climbed the ladder and Jack followed. It was almost dark inside, but the warm wood smelled like a summer day.

paragraphs.context: They glanced around the tree house. They saw
paragraphs.simple: They looked around. They saw the scrolls from Shakespeare's theater, the twig from the mountain gorillas, and the bag of corn seeds from the first Thanksgiving.

background.note: In book 25 Jack and Annie visited William Shakespeare's theater in London in 1601.
In book 27 they joined the Pilgrims' harvest feast in 1621.

paragraphs.context: Good luck on your fourth journey to find
paragraphs.simple: Morgan wished them good luck on their fourth trip to find a special magic. A secret rhyme will show them the way.

paragraphs.context: She shrugged. “Yep. I guess we have to
paragraphs.simple: Annie lifted her shoulders. She guessed they had to build a ship, but where?

paragraphs.context: She and Jack looked at the book’s cover.
paragraphs.simple: The cover showed palm trees, a beach and a beautiful ocean. The title was A Visit to Old Hawaii.

paragraphs.context: “How do you know you love it?” Jack
paragraphs.simple: Jack asked how Annie could love Hawaii. They had never been there.
paragraphs.tone: Jack always wants facts. Annie follows her feelings.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. A gentle wind brushed
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. A soft wind touched his skin. It smelled sweet and fresh.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out, too. The tree house had
paragraphs.simple: The tree house was on top of a tall palm tree at the edge of a field full of flowers.

paragraphs.context: On one side of the meadow, a cliff
paragraphs.simple: On one side of the field, a cliff went down to the beach. On the other side were the roofs of a small village.

paragraphs.context: Beyond the village were tall gray mountains. Misty
paragraphs.simple: Behind the village were tall gray mountains. Clouds hid their tops, and water fell down their sides.

paragraphs.context: “I have to learn about it first,” said
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he had to learn about Hawaii first. He opened the research book.

paragraphs.context: Hawaii is a chain of islands in the
paragraphs.simple: Hawaii is a chain of islands in the Pacific. The biggest island is also called Hawaii. Volcanoes under the sea made the islands millions of years ago.

paragraphs.context: The volcanic rock crumbled and turned to soil.
paragraphs.simple: The rock broke down and became soil. Wind and birds dropped seeds. Plants and trees grew, and birds and insects came to live.

paragraphs.context: About two thousand years ago, people first came
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first people came by canoe.
paragraphs.simple: About 2,000 years ago, people came to Hawaii in canoes from other Pacific islands. They traveled thousands of miles, using only the wind and stars to find the way.

background.term: They came in canoes from other islands
background.note: The first Hawaiians were Polynesians. They sailed big double canoes across thousands of miles of open sea.

paragraphs.context: Jack put down the book and listened. Sounds
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard music and laughter in the wind.

paragraphs.context: “We’ll figure that out later,” said Annie. “Let’s
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they would think about the ship later. Maybe the people at the party could help.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a whoop of laughter in the
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard a loud happy shout. The party sounded fun, he thought, so he followed Annie.

paragraphs.context: The sun was low in the sky. They
paragraphs.simple: The sun was low. They walked through the field toward the village. Everything was covered in golden red light.

paragraphs.context: There was beauty everywhere: purple flowers shaped like
paragraphs.simple: There was beauty everywhere: purple and white flowers, tall soft ferns, spiky plants, big butterflies and tiny yellow birds.

paragraphs.context: When they got close to the village, they
paragraphs.simple: Near the village, they saw lots of people. Jack and Annie hid behind a palm tree and looked secretly at the party.

paragraphs.context: There were about fifty people, including grown-ups, teenagers
paragraphs.simple: About fifty people were there: adults, teenagers and children. They had no shoes, and they wore rings of flowers around their necks.

paragraphs.context: A woman was chanting. Her words rose and
paragraphs.simple: A woman was chanting. Her words went up and down like waves. She chanted about Pele, the volcano goddess.

background.note: The goddess of volcanoes and fire in Hawaiian stories. People say she lives in the Kilauea volcano. Say it PEH-leh.

paragraphs.context: While she chanted, other people played music. Some
paragraphs.simple: Others played music: pipes like flutes, dried gourds that sounded like baby toys, and sticks that made clicking sounds.

paragraphs.context: Most of the villagers were dancing to the
paragraphs.simple: Most of the villagers were dancing. They stepped from side to side, moved their hips and waved their hands.

paragraphs.context: “They’re doing the hula,” whispered Annie. She smiled
paragraphs.simple: Annie whispered that they were doing the hula, and she waved her hands too.

background.note: A Hawaiian dance. The hand movements tell a story, like waves, rain or birds.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t get carried away,” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack told Annie not to get too excited.

paragraphs.context: The early Hawaiians had no written language. They
paragraphs.simple: The book said the early Hawaiians had no writing. They told stories with hula dancing, which mixes dancing and chanting poems.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly Jack heard loud laughter and clapping. He
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard laughing and clapping. He looked up and Annie was gone!

paragraphs.context: Jack peeked out from behind the tree. Annie
paragraphs.simple: Annie was dancing the hula with the dancers. Nobody was surprised. Everyone smiled at her.

paragraphs.context: A girl caught sight of Jack. She looked
paragraphs.simple: A girl about Annie's age saw Jack. She had long shiny black hair and a big friendly smile.

paragraphs.context: The girl didn’t let go. She pulled Jack
paragraphs.simple: The girl did not let go. She pulled Jack into the open. The dancers and musicians smiled at him.

paragraphs.context: Jack stood still. He didn’t know how to
paragraphs.simple: Jack stood without moving. He couldn't dance at all, and certainly not the hula! He looked at the ground and held his backpack and notebook until the music stopped.

paragraphs.context: The Hawaiians gathered around Jack and Annie. They
paragraphs.simple: The Hawaiians came around Jack and Annie. They all looked friendly.

paragraphs.context: “I’m Kama,” the girl said. “This is my
paragraphs.simple: The girl was Kama. Her brother Boka was about Jack's age.

paragraphs.context: The boy stepped forward. He grinned a big
paragraphs.simple: Boka smiled a big smile like his sister. He took off his ring of red flowers and put it around Annie's neck.

paragraphs.context: “A lei to welcome you,” Boka said.
paragraphs.simple: Boka said the lei was to welcome her.

background.note: A Hawaiian ring of flowers worn around the neck. People give leis to say welcome, goodbye or thank you.

paragraphs.context: But Jack broke in. “From over the mountains,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie started to say "Frog Creek", but Jack quickly said they came from over the mountains.

paragraphs.context: They’re all amazingly nice, Jack thought.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought they were all very nice.

paragraphs.context: She and Boka led Jack and Annie to
paragraphs.simple: Kama and Boka took them to the edge of the open space. They sat with crossed legs in the grass. Kama held out a wooden bowl.

paragraphs.context: “It is poi,” said Kama. She scooped some
paragraphs.simple: Kama said it was poi. She took some with her fingers and licked them.

background.note: A traditional Hawaiian food made from cooked taro root, pounded into a soft paste.

paragraphs.context: Jack stuck his finger in the bowl, too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tried poi. It felt like peanut butter, but it tasted strange: bitter and sweet.

paragraphs.context: “No, no,” said Jack. “It’s … ” He
paragraphs.simple: Jack tried to think of something nice to say. He said it was "very interesting".
paragraphs.tone: "Interesting" is what people say when they don't like something but want to be polite. Kama and Boka understand the joke.

paragraphs.context: “Interesting!” they exclaimed. They cracked up laughing. Jack
paragraphs.simple: Kama and Boka said "Interesting!" and laughed hard. Jack and Annie laughed too.

paragraphs.context: Kama’s friendly smile made Jack want to tell
paragraphs.simple: Kama's friendly smile made Jack want to tell her the truth.

paragraphs.context: “It’s actually called Frog Creek,” he said. “It’s
paragraphs.simple: Jack said their home was Frog Creek, very far away. They traveled in a magic tree house.

paragraphs.context: Kama’s and Boka’s eyes got huge. They smiled
paragraphs.simple: Kama's and Boka's eyes opened wide. They smiled even more.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, we are,” said Jack. He felt great
paragraphs.simple: Jack felt great telling his new friends about the tree house. He had never told his friends at home.

paragraphs.context: “Our mother invites you to sleep at our
paragraphs.simple: Kama's mother invited them to sleep at their house.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stood up. In the gray
paragraphs.simple: In the evening light, they walked through the village. They went in and out between small huts until Kama stopped.

paragraphs.context: The hut had no door—just a wide entrance
paragraphs.simple: The hut had no door, just a wide opening into one big room.

paragraphs.context: Kama and Boka led Jack and Annie inside.
paragraphs.simple: In the low light, Jack could just see walls of dried grass and grass mats on the earth floor.

paragraphs.context: He took off his shoes and wreath of
paragraphs.simple: Jack took off his shoes and flowers and used his backpack as a pillow. The wind moved the palm leaves. Music came softly from the party.

paragraphs.context: “Tomorrow we will take you wave riding,” said
paragraphs.simple: Boka said tomorrow they would take them wave riding.

paragraphs.context: “Cool,” said Jack. But he wasn’t sure he
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Cool", but he was not sure. Surfing seemed scary.

paragraphs.context: Soon Jack heard steady breathing. The other kids
paragraphs.simple: Soon Jack heard slow, even breathing. The other kids were asleep.

paragraphs.context: Oh darn, we forgot to ask them about
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought they forgot to ask about building a ship. They would ask tomorrow.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard pounding noises. He imagined Boka and
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard hitting sounds. He imagined Boka and Kama were building a ship.

paragraphs.context: He opened his eyes. Only he and Annie
paragraphs.simple: Only Jack and Annie were still in the hut. A cloth covered the doorway. Jack sat up and shook Annie.

paragraphs.context: Boka, Kama, and their parents smiled at Jack
paragraphs.simple: Boka, Kama and their parents smiled. They were all working, but no one was building a ship.

paragraphs.context: Boka was pounding a wide strip of bark
paragraphs.simple: Boka was hitting tree bark with a wooden stick. Kama was hitting a root like a fat sweet potato with a stone. Their parents were making grass mats.

paragraphs.context: “I’m making tapa,” said Boka. “First I beat
paragraphs.simple: Boka said he was making tapa. He beats mulberry bark into thin sheets. His father sticks the sheets together to make cloth.

background.note: The paper mulberry tree. Its inside bark was beaten flat to make tapa cloth.

paragraphs.context: “This is the root of a taro plant,”
paragraphs.simple: Kama said it was a taro root. If you add fruit, you get poi.

background.note: A plant with a big starchy root, also eaten in China (taro cakes, taro milk tea).

paragraphs.context: “Why would we do that?” asked Kama.
paragraphs.simple: Kama asked why they would sail away.
paragraphs.tone: Kama and Boka are happy on their island. They don't want to leave.

paragraphs.context: “Sure,” said Kama. While she showed Annie how
paragraphs.simple: Kama showed Annie how to pound taro. Jack went into the hut and added to his list about Hawaii.

paragraphs.context: “We’ve finished our chores,” said Kama. “May we
paragraphs.simple: Kama said they finished their jobs. She asked if they could take Jack and Annie to the ocean.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath. He half hoped their
paragraphs.simple: Jack stopped breathing. He partly hoped the parents would say no.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie followed Kama and Boka. They
paragraphs.simple: They passed busy villagers. Some carried wood or water. Others cut grass or took bark off trees.

paragraphs.context: Kama and Boka went into the grove of
paragraphs.simple: Kama and Boka went into the palm trees. They climbed up the leaning trunks with their hands and feet and shook the leaves.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie jumped back as big, round
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie jumped back as big round coconuts fell.

paragraphs.context: Kama and Boka slid down the trees. They
paragraphs.simple: Kama and Boka slid down. They hit the hard coconuts with rocks again and again until they broke in half.

paragraphs.context: Jack drank the fresh, sweet milk inside the
paragraphs.simple: Jack drank the fresh, sweet milk inside the coconut.

paragraphs.context: “Interesting?” asked Boka.
paragraphs.simple: Boka asked if it was "interesting". He remembered Jack's polite word for the poi.
paragraphs.tone: A friendly joke between new friends.

paragraphs.context: Then Kama picked bananas off a banana tree
paragraphs.simple: Kama picked bananas. Jack's was the best banana he ever ate.

paragraphs.context: When breakfast was over, they all headed into
paragraphs.simple: After breakfast, they walked into the field of flowers. The sky was very blue and the grass very green. Flowers and birds shone like jewels.

paragraphs.context: Hawaii is like a garden paradise, Jack thought.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought Hawaii was like a perfect garden.

paragraphs.context: Jack put away the book and hurried to
paragraphs.simple: Jack hurried to the others. He looked down at a beach fifty feet below.

paragraphs.context: There were no people. Only seashells and seaweed
paragraphs.simple: There were no people. Only shells and seaweed lay on the shining white sand. Big white waves crashed on the shore.

paragraphs.context: Uh-oh, thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: "Uh-oh," thought Jack.

paragraphs.context: Annie, Boka, and Kama started down the path.
paragraphs.simple: Annie, Boka and Kama went down the path. Jack followed slowly and carefully.

paragraphs.context: When he stepped onto the beach, Jack slipped
paragraphs.simple: On the beach, Jack took off his shoes. The warm dry sand felt as soft as silk.

paragraphs.context: “Actually, I wouldn’t mind just taking a walk
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he would be happy just to walk on the beach.

paragraphs.context: But no one seemed to hear. They had
paragraphs.simple: Nobody heard. They walked to a row of wooden surfboards leaning against the rocks.

paragraphs.context: Boka picked out a long board and lugged
paragraphs.simple: Boka chose a long board and carried it to Jack with effort.

paragraphs.context: Jack took the board and looked up at
paragraphs.simple: The board was as tall as Jack's dad.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. “I’d like to
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply and said he wanted to read about surfing first.

paragraphs.context: “How does it talk?” said Kama.
paragraphs.simple: Kama asked how the book talks.
paragraphs.tone: The early Hawaiians had no writing, so Kama has never seen a book.

paragraphs.context: “Jack, forget the book now,” Annie said. “Let’s
paragraphs.simple: Annie told Jack to forget the book and just do what Boka and Kama say.

paragraphs.context: “First we need to get past the breaking
paragraphs.simple: Kama said they first had to get past the waves that break near the shore.

paragraphs.context: Together they waded into the cool, shallow water.
paragraphs.simple: They walked into the cool, low water. Jack hoped the waves were not very big.

paragraphs.context: But as he waded deeper into the ocean
paragraphs.simple: As Jack went deeper, the waves looked bigger. The first wave almost knocked him over.

paragraphs.context: Kama, Boka, and Annie moved farther out into
paragraphs.simple: A big wave came over the others. They threw their boards over it and jumped into it.

paragraphs.context: Jack struggled forward. The next time a big
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved forward with difficulty. He threw his board over the next wave and went under it, holding his glasses.

paragraphs.context: Jack kept fighting his way forward. By the
paragraphs.simple: Jack kept fighting forward. When he got past the breaking waves, the water was up to his chest.

paragraphs.context: Boka and Kama pulled themselves onto their boards.
paragraphs.simple: Boka and Kama lay on their boards and paddled with their hands out to sea.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie lay down on their boards
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie did the same. Paddling over gentle waves, Jack felt calm. He could do this all day.

paragraphs.context: “When you start toward the shore!” said Boka.
paragraphs.simple: Boka said: stand up with one foot forward and put your arms out so you don't fall.

paragraphs.context: “But don’t try to stand up the very
paragraphs.simple: Kama said not to stand up the first time. Just ride lying down.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, wait!” said Jack. Everything was happening too
paragraphs.simple: Jack wanted them to wait. Everything was too fast, and he had questions.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw a big wave rolling toward them.
paragraphs.simple: A big wave rolled toward them. The others paddled fast. Jack paddled very hard to stay with them.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly the wave lifted him and swept him
paragraphs.simple: The wave lifted Jack and carried him forward very fast. At the side he saw Boka, Kama and Annie all standing up.
hardWords: Out of the corner of his eye

paragraphs.context: Jack wanted to be like them. In a
paragraphs.simple: Jack wanted to be like them. He quickly stood up. For one second he felt like a flying bird. Then he fell.

paragraphs.context: Jack fell into the water, grabbing his glasses
paragraphs.simple: Jack fell into the water. The wave crashed on him. Water went in his mouth and nose. His board and lei were carried away.

paragraphs.context: Jack twisted and turned in the churning water.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turned around in the wild water. When his head came up, he coughed.

paragraphs.context: Another big wave crashed down on him, and
paragraphs.simple: Another wave hit him and pushed him under. He moved forward hard, trying to get to the beach.

paragraphs.context: Again and again, Jack was thrown down and
paragraphs.simple: The waves threw him down again and again. Each time he got up and pushed himself closer to the beach.

paragraphs.context: Finally, Jack dragged himself out of the ocean.
paragraphs.simple: At last Jack pulled himself out of the ocean. He felt hurt and fell on the sand.

paragraphs.context: Jack just nodded. He put on his wet
paragraphs.simple: Jack felt weak and angry with himself. He should not have tried to stand.

paragraphs.context: “I told you not to stand,” she said
paragraphs.simple: Kama laughed and said she told him not to stand. He fell hard.

paragraphs.context: It’s not funny, thought Jack. I nearly drowned!
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not think it was funny. He almost died in the water.

paragraphs.context: “The best thing to do is to go
paragraphs.simple: Boka said the best thing is to go back into the water right away.
paragraphs.tone: This is good advice: after a fall, try again quickly so you don't become afraid.

paragraphs.context: “You go,” said Jack. His eyes and nose
paragraphs.simple: Jack's eyes and nose hurt from the salt water. He stayed on the beach and took out the book.

paragraphs.context: She ran to him and pulled the book
paragraphs.simple: Annie pulled the book out of Jack's hands. Jack pulled it back, slipped and fell.

paragraphs.context: “Why are you laughing?” Jack snapped. “You don’t
paragraphs.simple: Jack angrily said, "Why are you laughing? You can't even read!"

paragraphs.context: Boka and Kama looked hurt.
paragraphs.simple: Boka and Kama looked hurt.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his book and pretended to read
paragraphs.simple: Jack pretended to read. He did feel sorry, but he was too upset to say it.

paragraphs.context: As Jack sat alone on the beach, he
paragraphs.simple: Jack sat alone on the beach and watched the others paddling.

paragraphs.context: Morgan didn’t send us here to surf anyway
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought Morgan did not send them to surf. She told them to build a ship. How could they do that?

paragraphs.context: Jack heaved an angry sigh. Now he was
paragraphs.simple: Jack let out an angry breath. Now he was angry with Morgan. He looked for "ship" in the index.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly Jack heard a rumbling from under the
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly Jack heard a deep sound under the sand. The ground shook so hard that the book flew out of his hands.

paragraphs.context: Jack bounced up and down on the beach.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved up and down on the beach. Shells jumped too. Rocks fell from the cliff.

paragraphs.context: It’s an earthquake! thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought, "It's an earthquake!"
